items.title: Aborted takeoff
items.lede: A takeoff is aborted when an emergency or abnormal situation occurs during the takeoff roll that will require a pilot to abort the takeoff. The power is reduced to idle and sufficient braking applied to stop on the runway while also maintaining directional control.

items.title: Aircraft documentation and airworthiness
items.lede: The airworthiness of the airplane is determined in three general ways: compliance with recurrent inspections requirements, ready access to FAA required documentation, and a physical pre-flight. The ultimate decision on whether an aircraft is airworthy resides with the Pilot in Command (PIC).

items.title: Aircraft preflight inspection

references.loc: §405 — Outer Wing Surfaces and Tail Section

items.lede: A safe flight begins with a careful visual inspection of the airplane. The purpose of the preflight visual inspection is twofold: to determine that the airplane is legally airworthy, and that it is in condition for safe flight. The final determination of whether the airplane is in a condition for safe flight is made by a physical preflight inspection of the airplane and its components.

items.title: ATC light gun signals
items.lede: An airport control tower uses a directive traffic control signal which emits an intense narrow light beam of a selected color (either red, white, or green) to issue control instructions to aircraft with inoperative radios.

items.title: Class C airspace
items.lede: Class C airspace is generally that airspace from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL) surrounding those airports that have an operational control tower, are serviced by a radar approach control, and that have a certain number of IFR operations or passenger enplanements. Entry requires a two-way radio, a transponder with automatic altitude reporting, ADS-B Out, and two-way radio communications established with ATC before crossing the boundary.

items.title: Cloud clearances
items.lede: No person may operate an aircraft under basic VFR when the flight visibility is less, or at a distance from clouds that is less, than that prescribed for the corresponding altitude and class of airspace.

items.title: Crew resource management

references.loc: §206 — Crew Resource Management (CRM) Roles and Responsibilities

items.lede: Crew resource management is the effective use of all available resources by individuals, crews and teams to safely and efficiently accomplish the mission or task. It includes all crew members, equipment, and external factors involving the flight from before the flight brief to after the flight debrief. The human error factor, or inadequate CRM, is the single leading causal factor for Class A mishaps in modern naval aviation.

items.title: Crosswind landing

references.loc: §629 — Common Errors During Crosswind Approaches and Landings

items.lede: The same basic principles and factors involved in a normal approach and landing apply to a crosswind approach and landing, so only the additional procedures required for correcting for wind drift are different. The wing-down, top rudder (sideslip) method will compensate for a crosswind from any angle, and it enables the pilot to simultaneously keep the airplane's ground track and longitudinal axis aligned with the runway centerline throughout the final approach, roundout, touchdown, and after-landing roll. This prevents the airplane from touching down in a sideward motion and imposing damaging side loads on the landing gear. The drift is controlled with aileron and the heading with rudder. A maximum of 15 KIAS is the crosswind limitation for NIFE aircraft.

items.title: Electrical fire in flight
items.lede: A fire in flight demands immediate and decisive action. In-flight fires are classified as inflight engine fires, electrical fires, and cabin fires. The initial indication of an electrical fire is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation. The most prudent course of action is to land as soon as possible.

items.title: Emergency landing pattern

references.loc: §704 — Common Errors During Emergency Landing Patterns

items.lede: The ELP is a 360° pattern designed to position the aircraft for landing at a prepared surface during a complete power loss or when an impending engine failure exists in which sufficient power for continued flight is available. It is used for both actual and simulated emergency approaches and landings to a runway or a cleared area. The entire pattern is designed to be circular, but the turn may be shallowed, steepened, or discontinued at any point to adjust the accuracy of the flightpath.

items.title: Engine failure after takeoff

numbers.label: Field selection arc
numbers.value: 30 degrees either side of takeoff path

items.lede: What characterizes all power loss or engine failure occurrences after takeoff is urgency. In most instances, the pilot has only a few seconds after an engine failure to decide what course of action to take and to execute it. Unless prepared in advance to make the proper decision, there is an excellent chance the pilot will make a poor decision, or make no decision at all and allow events to rule.

items.title: Engine failure during flight
items.lede: An airplane forced down by engine failure is the typical example of a forced landing: an immediate landing, on or off an airport, necessitated by the inability to continue further flight. A pilot's choice of emergency landing sites is governed by the route selected during preflight planning, the height above the ground when the emergency occurs, and excess airspeed, which can be converted into distance and/or altitude. Above 1000 feet the Emergency Landing Procedure attempts a restart; below 1000 feet with no restart it goes to emergency shutdown and the emergency approach profile.

items.title: Engine fire during start

references.loc: NIFE Checklist — Engine Fire During Start
NIFE Checklist — Emergency Shutdown on Deck

items.lede: Engine compartment fires can be indicated by smoke and/or flames coming from the engine cowling area. Whether or not the engine starts, the procedure ends in Emergency Shutdown on Deck.

items.title: Engine run-up

events.label: Engine run up procedures and limitations

items.lede: The runup check is the systematic procedure for making a check of the engine, controls, systems, instruments, and avionics prior to flight. Normally, it is performed after taxiing to a general runup area or a position near the takeoff end of the runway.
terms: Engine run up procedures and limitations

items.title: 4 Ts
items.lede: The transition procedure is flown in four steps: **T**ransition, **T**rim, **T**urn, **T**alk. At a towered field, expect tower to clear you for landing before the Abeam position, which will take care of the fourth T.

items.title: I'M SAFE checklist
items.lede: External human factors refer to all the external happenings in a pilot's life that are not directly related to the safe operation of the aircraft. "I'M SAFE" is a simple checklist to determine if we are ready and fit to fly.

items.title: Instrument usage during VFR flying
items.lede: When introducing basic flight maneuvers to a beginning pilot, the "integrated flight instruction" or "composite" method will be used. This means that each flight maneuver will be performed by using both outside visual references and the flight instruments. At least 90 percent of the pilot's attention should be devoted to positioning the airplane in relation to the natural horizon, along with scanning for other airplanes, and no more than 10 percent of the pilot's attention should be inside the cockpit.

items.title: Level speed change

references.loc: §517 — Common Errors During Level Speed Change

items.lede: Maneuvering during slow flight demonstrates the flight characteristics and degree of controllability of an airplane at less than cruise speeds. The objective is to develop the pilot's sense of feel and ability to use the controls correctly, and to improve proficiency in performing maneuvers that require slow airspeeds.

items.title: Local area procedures
items.lede: The Letter of Agreement between Pensacola TRACON, Pensacola ATCT, Sky Warrior Flight Training Inc, Pensacola Air Flight School, the Navy Flying Club and US Navy Introductory Flight Evaluation (NIFE) provides standard VFR arrival and departure procedures for locally based training flights and describes areas to avoid (hot spots) in the local area. These procedures are for training flights to and from the Pensacola International Airport (PNS). Aircraft requesting the Northwest Practice Area can expect radar vectors to point LASKE or PAPER at 2,700 MSL on departure, and on return either radar vectors to final or the Northwest Arrival, depending on the runway in use.

items.title: Lost communication
items.lede: Radio malfunction procedures cover an inoperative transmitter and receiver or one of the other, in the air and on the taxiway. After extensive troubleshooting, squawk 7600 and proceed inbound to your destination while continuing to make all calls in the blind (making calls as if it still worked).

items.title: Normal takeoff and climb
items.lede: Although the takeoff and climb is one continuous maneuver, it is divided into three steps for purposes of explanation: the takeoff roll, the lift-off, and the initial climb after becoming airborne. The takeoff is made as nearly into the wind as possible, because the airplane's speed while on the ground is much less than if the takeoff were made downwind, and a shorter ground roll and therefore much less runway length is required to develop the minimum lift necessary for takeoff and climb.

items.title: Operational risk management
items.lede: Operational risk management is the process of dealing with the risk associated with military operations. The ORM process is a decision-making tool used by personnel at all levels to increase effectiveness by identifying, assessing, and managing risks. It is utilized on three levels based upon time and assets available, guided by four principles and worked through five steps. ORM shall be conducted prior to all NIFE flights using the NIFE ORM Worksheet.

items.title: Power, attitude, trim principle
items.lede: For corrections and to execute many maneuvers you must set or reset power, adjust the nose attitude, and trim for the new attitude. The mechanics of the transitions are performed in a specific sequence: **P**ower, **A**ttitude, **T**rim.

items.title: Power-off stall

references.loc: §524 — Use of Ailerons/Rudder During Stall Recovery

items.lede: A stall occurs when the smooth airflow over the airplane's wing is disrupted, and the lift degenerates rapidly. This is caused when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack, and can occur at any airspeed, in any attitude, with any power setting. The practice of power-off stalls is usually performed in the landing configuration simulating an accidental stall occurring during landing approaches.

items.title: Power-on stall
items.lede: Power-on stall recoveries are practiced from straight climbs to simulate an accidental stall occurring during takeoff climbs and departure climbs. Power-on stalls are practiced with the airplane in a clean configuration as in departure and normal climbs.

items.title: Any previously discussed item
items.lede: The discuss items briefed on earlier events, any of which can be asked. The list below is built from the syllabus.

items.title: Any previously discussed maneuver
items.lede: Maneuvers briefed on earlier events, any of which may be discussed on this event.

items.title: Racetrack pattern

references.loc: §618 — Common Errors During Normal Approach and Landing
§616 — Procedure for Touch and Go Landing

items.lede: The landing pattern is a geometric racetrack-shaped course flown so that an approach and landing may be executed in a systematic sequence. The landing line, the upwind leg, and the parallel downwind leg form the sides of the racetrack pattern. These lines are joined together by the crosswind turn and by the approach turn at the downwind end of the pattern. The racetrack pattern is a military style pattern, while most civilians fly a rectangular (box) pattern. It is flown from the downwind leg through the abeam position, the 180 and the 90 to the groove, and then through the flare, the touchdown and the after-landing roll.

items.title: Runway incursion avoidance
items.lede: A runway incursion is any occurrence at an airport involving an aircraft, vehicle, person, or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or results in a loss of separation with an aircraft taking off, landing, or intending to land.

items.title: Scan pattern and sight picture
items.lede: A scan pattern is a means or procedure by which you can observe everything you need to see by starting at one point, moving visually about the aircraft, checking all applicable items systematically and thoroughly, and completing the pattern at the starting point. A scan pattern may be started anywhere, but it must be complete and continuous. Contact flying, or attitude flying, means visually establishing the airplane's attitude with reference to ground references and the natural horizon.

items.title: See and avoid doctrine
items.lede: All pilots must be alert to the potential for midair collision and near midair collisions. The general operating and flight rules in 14 CFR part 91 set forth the concept of "See and Avoid," which requires that vigilance shall be maintained at all times, by each person operating an aircraft regardless of whether the operation is conducted under instrument or visual meteorological conditions. Simply stated, the "See and Avoid" Doctrine is a pilot's best defense against a midair collision.

items.title: Slip to land
items.lede: A slip occurs when the aircraft yaws towards the outside of a turn. An intentional slip requires deliberate cross-controlling ailerons and rudder throughout the maneuver, and is used to dissipate altitude without increasing airspeed, and/or to adjust airplane ground track during a crosswind. In a sideslip the airplane's longitudinal axis remains parallel to the original flightpath; in a forward slip the nose is yawed opposite the bank so that the longitudinal axis is at an angle to the original flightpath. Always announce the slip, "(Left/Right) wing down, (Left/Right) top rudder."

items.title: Standard operating procedures

references.loc: §206 — Crew Resource Management (CRM) Roles and Responsibilities

items.lede: The NIFE SOP promulgates standard operating procedures for ground and flight operations within the NIFE course. It supplements the Master Curriculum Guide, the FTI and the Inflight Guide, and provides guidance in the event that no other governing directive applies. Should conflict exist between it and any other publication, the more restrictive directive will govern. Only the Commanding Officer or his representative may approve deviations from it.

items.title: Takeoff brief
items.lede: Prior to taking the runway a concise takeoff brief shall be conducted. The takeoff brief ensures the student and instructor have clearly defined roles and have discussed a plan should an emergency occur during this critical phase of flight.

items.title: Towered operations and CTAF
items.lede: The flow of communications at a non-towered field mirrors that of a towered field. At a towered airport, surface operations are controlled by a member of the local ATC service team referred to as the ground controller, and the tower issues the clearance to take the runway and the clearance to land. At a non-towered field, all communications happen on the same Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF), all communications are in the form of a self-announcement (broadcast) of the pilot's intentions, and pilots are responsible for ensuring that their takeoff will not interfere with landing traffic.

items.title: Traffic pattern
items.lede: An airport traffic pattern is established appropriate to the local conditions, including the direction and placement of the pattern, the altitude to be flown, and the procedures for entering and leaving the pattern. Unless the airport displays approved visual markings indicating that turns should be made to the right, the pilot should make all turns in the pattern to the left. The standard traffic pattern altitude is usually 1,000 feet above the elevation of the airport surface.

items.title: Turn pattern
items.lede: The objective of the turn pattern is to develop smoothness, coordination, orientation, and division of attention. Smoothness of control use, coordination, and accuracy of execution are the important features of this maneuver. It is started at 90 KIAS on any cardinal heading and consists of two 15° AOB turns in opposite directions for 30° of heading change, two 30° AOB turns in opposite directions for 90° of heading change, and two 45° AOB turns in opposite directions for 180° of heading change.

items.title: Wake turbulence and wind shear

references.loc: §4-3-7 — Low Level Wind Shear/Microburst Detection Systems

items.lede: Every aircraft generates a wake while in flight, caused by a pair of counter-rotating vortices trailing from the wing tips. The vortices from larger aircraft pose problems to encountering aircraft such as severe rolling moments while near the ground. In general, avoid the area below and behind the generating aircraft, especially at low altitude where even a momentary wake encounter could be hazardous. Wind shear is a change in wind speed and/or wind direction in a short distance, and it can exist in a horizontal or vertical direction and occasionally in both.

items.title: Waveoff
items.lede: Whenever landing conditions are not satisfactory, a waveoff is warranted. The waveoff is not strictly an emergency procedure. It is a normal maneuver that may at times be used in an emergency situation, and like any other normal maneuver it must be practiced and perfected. The improper execution of the waveoff maneuver stems from a lack of familiarity with the three cardinal principles of the procedure: power, attitude, and configuration.
